name: Narcotics Anonymous (NA)
description: Community-based program for people recovering from drug addiction. 12-step fellowship with meetings worldwide.

sections.title: About Narcotics Anonymous
sections.text: Narcotics Anonymous (NA) is a global, community-based organization with a multilingual and multicultural membership. Founded in 1953, NA offers recovery from the effects of addiction through working a twelve-step program including regular attendance at group meetings. The only requirement for membership is a desire to stop using drugs. NA makes no distinction between drugs including alcohol—the focus is on addiction as a disease that affects every area of life. NA is not affiliated with any treatment centers, religions, political organizations, or institutions.

sections.title: How NA Works
sections.text: NA is a program of complete abstinence from all drugs. The Twelve Steps of NA provide a framework for personal recovery that addresses the physical, mental, and spiritual aspects of addiction. Members work through these steps with the support of a sponsor—an experienced member who has worked the steps themselves. Regular meeting attendance, phone contact with other members, and service work are key components. NA emphasizes that addiction is a disease, not a moral failing, and that recovery is possible through mutual support and spiritual growth.

sections.title: Finding NA Meetings
sections.text: NA has more than 70,000 weekly meetings in 144 countries worldwide. Meetings are held in-person at various community locations and online through virtual meeting platforms. Visit na.org and use the meeting search tool to find meetings near you. Meeting formats include open meetings (anyone can attend), closed meetings (for addicts only), speaker meetings, discussion meetings, step study, and tradition study groups. Most areas have meetings available every day of the week, often multiple times per day.

sections.title: What to Expect at Your First Meeting
sections.text: NA meetings are welcoming to newcomers. Meetings typically open with readings from NA literature, followed by sharing from members or a speaker. You are never required to speak, introduce yourself, or share anything personal. What you hear at meetings is confidential. Many meetings have a newcomer's welcome where first-time visitors can ask questions. You may be offered phone numbers from members willing to talk between meetings. There are no dues or fees—NA is entirely self-supporting through member contributions.

sections.title: Getting Started in NA
sections.text: If you think you may have a problem with drugs, NA suggests attending several meetings to get a feel for the program. Each meeting has its own atmosphere, so trying different groups can help you find where you feel comfortable. Consider getting a sponsor—someone to guide you through the steps and answer questions. NA literature, including the Basic Text and informational pamphlets, provides detailed information about the program. Many areas have helplines staffed by NA members who can answer questions and provide meeting information. The NA website also offers online resources and virtual meetings.
